title: The Armistice, 1918 — the soldier killed one minute before the war ended
sources: Wikipedia: Armistice of 11 November 1918 — signed in a railroad car in the Compiègne Forest; agreed at 5:00 a.m., signatures between 5:00 and 5:45 a.m. Paris time; in effect at 11:00 a.m. Paris time, "the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month"; the German delegation was headed by Matthias Erzberger, aboard Foch's private train; many artillery units kept firing to avoid hauling away spare ammunition; 10,944 casualties, of whom 2,738 men died, on the last day of the war

Wikipedia: Henry Gunther — from Baltimore; supply sergeant, demoted after a critical letter home about "miserable conditions" was intercepted by the censor; at Chaumont-devant-Damvillers he charged a roadblock of two German machine guns against his sergeant's orders; the Germans, aware of the armistice, tried to wave him away; killed at 10:59 a.m., about one minute before the armistice; James M. Cain wrote that he was determined "to make good"; Pershing's order of the day named him the last American killed in the war; the Army posthumously restored his rank of sergeant
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1880 Ned Kelly is hanged in Melbourne; 1920 the Cenotaph is unveiled in London and the Unknown Warrior buried in Westminster Abbey
Film: "La journée de l'Armistice" (Paris, 11 November 1918), CC0 via Wikimedia Commons

Images (public domain / CC0): the signing in the railway carriage (painting); Foch's train; the signed armistice; US 64th Infantry celebrating; New York crowds announcing the armistice; The New York Times, 11 November 1918; German prisoners, Hundred Days Offensive; Armistice Day in London

post.facebook:
On this day in 1918, the First World War ended — at 11 o'clock.

Germany signed the armistice at 5 a.m. in Marshal Foch's railway carriage in the Compiègne Forest. But the ceasefire was set for 11:00 a.m. — "the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month". Until then, the fighting went on; many artillery units fired off their spare ammunition rather than haul it away. On that last day there were 10,944 casualties, and 2,738 men died.

At 10:59, Henry Gunther of Baltimore — demoted after a letter home about the misery at the front was intercepted — charged a German machine-gun post. The German soldiers, who knew the armistice was a minute away, tried to wave him off. He kept going, and was killed. General Pershing named him the last American killed in the war, and the Army gave him back his rank of sergeant.

Also on 11 November: Ned Kelly was hanged in Melbourne (1880), and London buried its Unknown Warrior (1920).
